extracted.intended_audience: technically oriented readers (mathematicians, programmers, and non-specialists) interested in formalizing and verifying mathematical proofs using Metamath
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for expressing, verifying, and using fully formalized mathematical proofs in the Metamath language and program; discusses strengths, limitations, pedagogical uses, and practical trade-offs of formalization. Useful for people deciding when and how to formalize mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability for machine verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath makes abstract mathematics more concrete. It allows a computer to keep track of the complexity associated with each word or symbol with absolute rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof is expressed in the Metamath language it can be traced step-by-step back to axioms and verified by a program; formalizability gives any reader (not only experts) the ability to verify proofs themselves. This is presented as a core desideratum for trustworthy mathematics: the ability for a computer to check every inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and small language specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification of the Metamath language is only four pages long (Section 4.1). Its simplicity is a deliberate design feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal language for proofs should be compact and simple enough to learn quickly, yet powerful enough to express mathematics. Simplicity aids understanding and trust by reducing hidden machinery; the text warns that apparent simplicity might seem surprising but is sufficient for low-level symbol manipulations implicit in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by symbol substitution only
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program does not have the built-in ability to make logical inferences; it just makes a series of symbol substitutions according to instructions given to it in a proof and verifies that the result matches the expected theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs supplied to the program must include the substitution steps (instructions). The verifier checks that substitutions follow from declared axioms/rules; it does not invent or infer new steps beyond what is encoded. This clarifies the model of proof-checking and what is required of authored proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability to axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: After learning Metamath’s basic statement types, any technically oriented person can immediately trace any theorem proved in the language as far back as he or she wants, all the way to the axioms on which the theorem is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traceability is highlighted as a benefit: anyone can investigate individual proof steps to any desired depth without relying on expert intuition. For pedagogy and personal verification, being able to step down to axioms is valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate domain: best for abstract/pure mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although in principle Metamath can be used with any kind of mathematics, it is best suited for abstract or 'pure' mathematics that is mostly concerned with theorems and their proofs, as opposed to mathematics that deals with practical manipulation of numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of suitable branches: logic, set theory, number theory, group theory, abstract algebra, analysis, topology. For fields relying heavily on abstract theorems and symbolic reasoning, Metamath is well matched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not suited for intensive numeric computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath is less suited to applications that deal primarily with intensive numeric computations: it does not have any built-in representation of numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers must be constructed syntactically as strings when needed, so Metamath is best for symbolic/theoretical results where numbers are occasional constants. For heavy numeric or algebraic computation, use specialized tools (e.g., macsyma, Mathematica, Maple, Octave). This is an explicit design trade-off (simplicity vs built-in numeric support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design trade-offs consciously chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of built-in numbers was a conscious decision to help achieve Metamath’s simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/designers should accept and document trade-offs: simplicity can limit certain applications but make the system more general and easier to verify and understand for its intended domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of formal detail vs. human practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing proofs in the Metamath language is challenging, requiring a degree of rigor far in excess of that normally taught to students; the time needed to work out the details would not allow a course to cover much material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Metamath yields absolute correctness, the labor cost is high; in classroom settings formalizing all proofs may be impractical. Use Metamath in conjunction with traditional methods rather than as a wholesale replacement for informal homework in many teaching contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proofs provide rigorous error prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to attempt to derive your own results, Metamath will not let you make a mistake in reasoning. Even professional mathematicians make mistakes; Metamath makes it possible to thoroughly verify that proofs are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal verification is presented as a primary motivation: produces instant feedback and prevents subtle reasoning errors. This is a key advantage when validating claims (e.g., to check a purported proof by a non-expert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal mathematical language omits detail and uses hidden context
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe modern abstract mathematics, a terse informal language is used which despite its elegance is very difficult to learn. This informal language often has omitted detail and symbols with hidden context that are implicitly understood by an expert but few others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing expository mathematics, be aware that relying on implicit context and omitted steps excludes non-specialists. Formalization can expose and remove these hidden assumptions, improving accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formalization to increase accessibility for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath could make pure mathematics accessible to people who are not sufficiently skilled to figure out the implicit detail in ordinary textbook proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to trace and verify proof steps means hobbyists, programmers, and intelligent laypersons can explore and verify theorems without the long apprenticeship traditionally required; formalization can therefore democratize access to advanced mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits: proofs-from-first-principles may be infeasibly long
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a theorem in the primitive notation of set theory that corresponds to the arithmetic theorem ‘1000 + 2000 = 3000’. The formula would be forbiddingly long... Even quite basic theorems would demand almost unbelievably vast books to display their proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and system designers must recognize that formal derivations from the most primitive axioms can explode in length; this is a practical constraint on using foundational formalisms as the only source. It motivates using libraries, definitions, and higher-level lemmas to manage proof size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metatheorems and additional axioms may be required
rubrics_metrics.description: Many important theorems (deduction theorem, substitution theorem, completeness theorem) cannot be derived directly from the basic axioms and require 'metalogic' or are treated as complex additional axioms in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalization projects should expect to formalize meta-level results or adopt them as part of the working basis; this increases the size/complexity of the verifier and the proof corpus, and may require encoding higher-level reasoning principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal systems must manage growing complexity of metatheory
rubrics_metrics.description: It looks like the further along you get, the more 'axioms' you have to add, as each new theorem seems to involve additional 'metamathematical' reasoning that hasn't been formalized, and none of it can be derived from the axioms of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a project grows, the verifier and library tend to become larger and more intricate; anticipate maintenance, potential bugs, and the need to validate metatheorems. This is an anti-pattern for naive attempts to fully formalize mathematics without modularization and library reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verification requires explicit programming of inference principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A month later, you’ve spent much of your free time getting the computer to verify proofs in propositional calculus. You’ve programmed in the axioms, but you’ve also had to program in the deduction theorem, the substitution theorem, and the completeness theorem of propositional calculus, which by now you’ve resigned yourself to treating as rather complex additional axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building a proof verifier or formal corpus, be prepared to encode nontrivial inference principles as part of the system rather than assuming they are derivable; document these choices and their consequences for trust and proof size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization complements rather than replaces informal learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Used in conjunction with traditional methods, Metamath could make pure mathematics accessible to people who are not sufficiently skilled to figure out the implicit detail in ordinary textbook proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine formal verification with standard pedagogy: use Metamath to check and deepen understanding where helpful, but recognize that hand-based informal exercises may remain necessary for covering breadth in courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of computer-checkable proofs for adjudicating extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: With easily accessible computer-based abstract mathematics, a mathematician could say to a crank, 'don't bother me until you've demonstrated your claim on the computer!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal proofs serve as an objective arbiter for contested claims; requiring machine-checkable demonstrations raises the bar for extraordinary proofs and filters out flawed informal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: General applicability: expressivity across theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath is powerful and general enough so that virtually any mathematical theory, from the most basic to the deeply abstract, can be described with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a formal system, evaluate its expressivity: Metamath claims broad coverage, which is a criterion favoring adoption for a wide range of formalization projects despite practical size/cost trade-offs.
